content: Acute chest syndrome is characterized by the presence of a new infiltrate on a chest radiograph, accompanied by one or more symptoms such as fever, cough, sputum production, rapid breathing (tachypnoea), difficulty breathing (dyspnoea), or newly developed low oxygen levels (hypoxia). In individuals with sickle cell disease, the symptoms and complications of acute chest syndrome can vary significantly, whether the cause is infectious or non-infectious. Lung infections are more commonly observed in children, whereas infarction is more frequently seen in adults. However, these two processes are often interconnected and may occur simultaneously. The differences in the clinical presentation and severity of acute chest syndrome suggest that it may have multiple underlying causes. Effective treatment primarily relies on high-quality supportive care. Despite extensive research into the syndrome and its management, the outcomes of conventional treatments, including antibiotics, anticoagulants, and other therapies, have been largely unsatisfactory. Recently, there has been growing interest in the potential use of inhaled nitric oxide as a treatment option for acute chest syndrome. Nitric oxide is believed to play a critical role in regulating vascular smooth muscle tone at the cellular level and in preventing platelet aggregation (clumping). The pathophysiology of sickle cell disease aligns with a mechanism involving nitric oxide depletion. Although significant research has been conducted on the pathophysiology of acute chest syndrome, the therapeutic role of inhaled nitric oxide in this context remains uncertain. The objective of this research was to evaluate the effectiveness of inhaled nitric oxide in treating acute chest syndrome by comparing its impact on symptom improvement and clinical outcomes against standard care. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Haemoglobinopathies Trials Register, which includes references from extensive electronic database searches and manual reviews of relevant journals and conference proceedings. Additional searches were performed in July 2007 on clinical trial registries such as ClinicalTrials.gov, the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, Current Controlled Trials, and Clinicaltrials.com. The most recent search of the Haemoglobinopathies Trials Register was conducted on September 10, 2010. The inclusion criteria for this review required randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials involving individuals with sickle cell disease and acute chest syndrome. These trials needed to compare the use of inhaled nitric oxide with either a placebo or standard care, for any single or multiple treatment regimens, over any duration of time. However, no studies meeting these criteria were identified. As a result, no eligible studies were included in this review. The authors concluded that there is a pressing need for well-designed and adequately powered randomized controlled trials to evaluate the benefits and risks of inhaled nitric oxide as an adjunctive treatment to established therapies for acute chest syndrome.
